question: You are building a DCF model. Free cash flows: Year 1: ₹100 crore, Year 2: ₹120 crore, Year 3: ₹140 crore. Discount rate is 10%. What is the total present value of these three cash flows?
before: PV(Y1) = 100/1.10 = 90.91, PV(Y2) = 120/1.21 = 99.17, PV(Y3) = 140/1.331 = 105.19. Total = ₹295.27 crore. A is the undiscounted sum. C over-discounts. D is incorrect.
after:
Formula: PV = FCF₁/(1+r)¹ + FCF₂/(1+r)² + FCF₃/(1+r)³, where PV = present value of cash flows, FCF_t = free cash flow in year t, r = discount rate (10%), and t = year.

Step-by-step:

Year 1: PV = 100 / (1.10)¹ = 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.91 crore

Year 2: PV = 120 / (1.10)² = 120 / 1.21 = ₹99.17 crore

Year 3: PV = 140 / (1.10)³ = 140 / 1.331 = ₹105.19 crore

Total PV = 90.91 + 99.17 + 105.19 = ₹295.27 crore

Result: ₹295.27 crore

Why this is correct: The present value of future cash flows must discount each year's amount by the appropriate power of (1 + discount rate). Option B correctly applies the time value of money formula to each cash flow and sums them to arrive at the intrinsic value today.

Why the others are wrong:

A (₹360.00 crore): This is the simple undiscounted sum of the three cash flows (100 + 120 + 140). It ignores the time value of money entirely and overstates the present value by failing to account for the 10% discount rate.

C (₹280.42 crore): This figure results from using an incorrect discount rate or applying excessive discounting (e.g., using a rate higher than 10% or compounding the discount incorrectly). It under-values the cash flows relative to the proper 10% rate.

D (₹312.75 crore): This appears to result from a calculation error, possibly discounting some years incorrectly or using inconsistent compounding periods. It is neither the undiscounted sum nor the correct present value.

Intuition: In DCF valuation, every rupee received in the future is worth less today due to opportunity cost and risk. The discount rate (here 10%) reflects your required return; higher discount rates compress present values more sharply. A common analyst mistake is forgetting to compound the denominator by the correct power each year—this template error leads directly to option C.
